result.summary: A set of Pindar's fragments in different choral genres. A dithyramb invites the gods to Athens to honour Dionysos (Bromios), a processional hymn praises the island of Delos where Leto gave birth, and a dance-song addresses the Sun during an eclipse, praying that its omen be good for Thebes.

scenes.title: Editor's note on fragment classes
scenes.summary: The editor explains the kinds of Pindar's lost songs into which the fragments are grouped.

scenes.title: Dithyramb summoning gods to Athens
scenes.summary: The singer calls the Olympian gods to the Athenian dance and sings of Bromios, the sons of Kadmeän mothers, and the spring festival with violets and songs for Semele.

scenes.title: Hymn to Delos
scenes.summary: Delos is hailed as the sea's daughter and the star of the gods; once it drifted, until four pillars rose to support it when Leto gave birth there.
scenes.stakes: Leto in labour needs a fixed place to give birth.

scenes.title: Prayer to the eclipsed Sun
scenes.summary: The singer asks the Sun why it has hidden itself at midday, prays that the sign bring good to Thebes, and lists possible disasters he would endure.
scenes.stakes: Thebes and all people may face war, famine, storm or the destruction of mankind.

alias_notes.explanation: Leto is identified by her father's name, Koios.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid address to the Sun during an eclipse, expressing awe and fear.

analysis.text: The fragments show how song joins gods, places and community, from Athenian festival to Delian birth-myth to civic fear.
The eclipse song probably reflects the eclipse of 463 BC, showing how Greeks read celestial events as omens for their city.

fun_facts.text: Nearly two-thirds of Pindar's fragments cannot be assigned to any genre.

language_notes.text: Bromios means 'the roaring one', a title of Dionysus; the 'centre-stone' is the omphalos-like altar centre of Athens, filled with incense.
The offspring of the Highest (Zeus) and Kadmeän mothers are Dionysus (son of Semele) and Heracles (son of Alcmena), born of Theban women, descendants of Kadmos.
'Chamber of the Hours' is the opening of the seasons' storehouse; spring is imagined as released from a room guarded by the Hours.
'Earth-shoot' means an offshoot or sprout of the earth, here the island Delos, birthplace of Apollo and Artemis.
'She of Koios' is Leto, daughter of the Titan Koios. Delos once floated, and she found there the only refuge to bear Apollo and Artemis.
'Adamantine' means unbreakable, made of the hardest imagined substance.
'Wings of their strength' means men's powers of action, rendered useless by the sudden darkness.
'Emptying of the sea upon the earth' suggests a great flood. The list of calamities is what the eclipse might portend.

context_notes.text: Pindar's surviving complete odes are victory odes; these fragments come from other genres, known only through quotations by later writers.
Semele, mother of Dionysus by Zeus, was a Theban princess; the spring festival honours her and her son.
A hyporchema was a lively choral song with dance. This eclipse was visible at Thebes, Pindar's home city.

literary_notes.text: The repeated 'then' builds a rhythm of spring's arrival, piling up flowers, roses, flutes and hymns.
The island is made to drift and then be fixed by pillars rising from the earth, a mythic image of Delos's stability.
The poet addresses the Sun directly, questioning it as a living being and giving his alarm a personal urgency.
The long list of possible disasters, ending in resignation, shows the dread the eclipse inspires and the singer's courage.
